summary: Describes using the Common Open Policy Service protocol to provision policy to network devices. This document is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A manager sends rule sheets to network devices so they all follow the same rules. This describes that for one protocol. It is now old.

questions: how does a policy server configure devices
what is a policy information base
how do network policies roll back on error
subtitle: Use the COPS protocol to send policy configurations to network devices.

tldr.problem: Network devices must be configured with consistent policies (QoS rules, access controls, etc.), but configuration must adapt as policies change and as devices change their capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: COPS-PR extends the COPS protocol to let a policy server push named policy data to policy-aware devices, with transaction semantics so all policies succeed or all fail together.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic; policy-based networking has largely been superseded by simpler configuration management approaches, though the design principles remain relevant.

today: RFC 2748 (COPS base protocol) is Historic, and RFC 3084 is also Historic. Policy-based networking, while theoretically sound, proved too complex for widespread adoption. Modern networks typically use simpler configuration management (NETCONF, YANG) or cloud-native orchestration systems. However, the design principles—centralized policy, atomic transactions, explicit error reporting—remain influential in network management architecture.

sections.title: The Policy Provisioning Problem
sections.content:
Network devices such as routers and switches must enforce policies: rules that determine how traffic is handled, which addresses are allowed, what quality of service each flow gets, and so on. Before COPS-PR, policies were pushed through ad-hoc methods like SNMP or manual configuration. This document describes a scalable, transaction-oriented approach using the COPS (Common Open Policy Service) protocol to provision policies in bulk from a Policy Decision Point (PDP) server to Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) devices.

The provisioning model differs from the outsourcing model (where each request triggers a decision): instead, a PDP proactively sends policy updates to a PEP, and the PEP applies them. This works well for policies defined in Service Level Agreements (SLAs) that change infrequently, such as QoS configurations for a DiffServ network or access control rules for a border router.
sections.plainLanguage: A central manager (PDP) pushes rule sheets to devices (PEPs). The devices report back whether the rules worked. If rules are wrong, they roll back to the old rules.

sections.title: Policy Information Base Structure
sections.content:
Policies are organized in a Policy Information Base (PIB), a conceptual tree of policy data structures. Each structure type is a Provisioning Class (PRC); each instance is a Provisioning Instance (PRI). For example, a PRC might be a filter class and each PRI a single filter rule. A Provisioning Instance Identifier (PRID) uniquely names each instance within a scope.

A PIB can be extended with new PRCs, attributes can be added or deprecated, and existing PRCs can be extended by other PIBs. These changes are backward-compatible: a newer PEP working with an older PDP simply ignores unknown PRCs, while an older PEP working with a newer PDP reports errors and rolls back if it receives unsupported data.

Two COPS operations work on PRIs: Install (create or update an instance) and Remove (delete one or more instances by name or prefix). A single decision message can install some PRIs and remove others, and is treated as an atomic transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Policies are organized as a tree: classes of rules and specific rule instances. A manager can install, update, or delete rules. If any rule fails, all of them roll back.

sections.title: Message Exchange and State Management
sections.content:
When a device boots, it opens a TCP connection to its Policy Decision Point and sends a configuration request with device capabilities and current policy state. The PDP responds with a decision message containing the appropriate policies for that device. The device reports success or failure in a report message.

After this initial sync, the device keeps the request state open. If the device's capabilities change (e.g., a network interface goes up or down), it sends an updated request. The PDP asynchronously sends new or modified policies via additional decision messages. Each decision message is either installed (create/update) or removed, and the device always acknowledges with a report.

If the device cannot install a decision, it must roll back to the last good state. The PDP can also command the device to open a new request state (for a different policy domain) or close an existing one via special Request-State flags.
sections.plainLanguage: Device boots, tells manager its name and what it can do, manager sends rules. When rules change, manager sends new rules. When device breaks, it says so and goes back to the old rules.

sections.title: Data Encoding and Error Handling
sections.content:
Policy data is encoded using Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and carried in COPS objects. Each object has a header (length, S-Num, and S-Type) followed by the data. Key objects include:

PRID (Complete Provisioning Instance Identifier): Encodes the name of a policy instance using the same format as SNMP Object Identifiers.

PPRID (Prefix PRID): Used in remove operations to delete all instances matching a prefix (e.g., all filters of a certain class).

EPD (Encoded Provisioning Instance Data): Contains the actual policy values as a sequence of BER-encoded attributes.

Error objects: Global Provisioning Error Objects (GPERR) report device-wide errors (memory exhausted), while Class Provisioning Error Objects (CPERR) report class-specific problems (bad attribute value). Each error has a code and optional sub-code to identify the problematic attribute or class.
sections.plainLanguage: Policies are encoded as names and values, packed into UDP-sized messages. If something fails, the error message says what went wrong.

sections.title: Common Implementation Scenarios
sections.content:
COPS-PR assumes different roles for different network entities:

Simple e-mailers and border routers: These inject policy data proactively when their configuration changes.

E-mail forwarders and mailing list servers: These rewrite message headers or addresses to pass sender authentication checks, then provision policies to reflect the new addressing.

Third-party mailers: These send mail on behalf of other users and provision their own policies under their control.

In all cases, the PDP maintains a view of each PEP's installed policies and can update them when business policy changes (new SLA, new security rules, etc.) without requiring the PEP to reboot or reconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: Different services (routers, mail servers, filters) each talk to the manager. The manager keeps track of what rules are on each device.
